title: Increasing Order Search Tree
statement:
You get `root`, the root of a binary search tree (every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's value, and every value in its right subtree is larger).

Rebuild the tree into a single path that only goes right and visits the values in increasing order: the node with the smallest value becomes the new root, no node has a left child, and each node's right child is the node with the next larger value (the largest node has no right child). Return the new root.
constraints: The tree has between 1 and 100 nodes
root is a valid binary search tree
notes:
## Intuition

In a binary search tree, an in-order walk (left subtree, node, right subtree) meets the values in increasing order. So the answer is simply the nodes in in-order sequence, each hung on the right of the one before. A brute-force alternative collects all values, sorts them and builds new nodes, but it costs O(n log n) and extra nodes; the in-order walk relinks the existing nodes in O(n).

## Approach

1. Create a placeholder node `dummy` and let `tail` point to it; `tail` is the last node of the chain built so far.
2. `visit(node)` walks the tree in order. An empty subtree does nothing.
3. First visit the left subtree, so every smaller value is already in the chain.
4. Then clear `node.left`, attach `node` as `tail.right` and move `tail` to `node`.
5. Finally visit the right subtree, whose values all come after `node`.
6. After `visit(root)`, the chain starts at `dummy.right`; return it.

## Example 1, step by step

The walk goes down the left side from `5` to `3`, `2` and `1`. Node `1` has no left child, so it is attached first: `dummy → 1`, `tail = 1`. Back at `2`: `1 → 2`. Back at `3`: `2 → 3`, then its right child `4`: `3 → 4`. Back at the root: `4 → 5`. The right side gives `6`, then `7` (left child of `8`), `8` and `9`. The chain is `1 → 2 → ... → 9` and `dummy.right` is node `1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n), every node is visited once and relinked in constant time.
- Space: O(h) for the recursion, where h is the tree's height (up to n for a one-sided tree).

## Pitfalls

- Clear `node.left` when attaching a node, or old left links remain and the result is not a chain.
- Read `node.right` only after attaching `node`: here `visit(node.right)` still sees the original right child, because attaching changes `tail.right`, not `node.right`.
- Without the `dummy` node, the very first attachment needs a special case to remember the new root.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dummy` | placeholder before the first real node of the chain |
| `tail` | last node attached to the chain so far |
| `visit` | in-order walk that attaches each node to the chain |
| `node` | root of the subtree being visited |

narration.2: A placeholder node in front of the chain, so the first real node needs no special case.
narration.3: tail always points at the last node added to the chain.
narration.4: visit walks a subtree in order: left part, the node, right part.
narration.5: An empty subtree adds nothing to the chain.
narration.8: Attach every smaller value first by visiting the left subtree.
narration.9: In the chain no node has a left child, so drop this one's.
narration.10: Hang the node right after the current end of the chain.
narration.11: This node is now the end of the chain.
narration.12: Every larger value in this subtree comes next, so visit the right subtree.
narration.14: Start the in-order walk from the original root.
narration.15: The smallest node sits right after the placeholder; it is the new root.
